title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
claim: Our approximate cross-validation matches the accuracy of exact selection criteria while running orders of magnitude faster, at every scale.
layout: 3x3 grid of line plots, columns by dimension, rows by metric, shared legend
description: A 3-by-3 grid of line plots with markers. Columns are labeled p: 100, p: 200 and p: 500. Rows show TPR, FDR and computation time in seconds on a log scale. The x-axis is sample size n (x100), from 0 to 50. Four methods are compared: ACV_Kfold (pink diamonds, solid line), BIC (orange triangles, dashed), CV_Kfold (green circles, dash-dot) and EBIC (purple squares, dash-dot). The legend sits at the bottom. In the TPR row, all methods rise to 1.0 as n grows, and EBIC rises more slowly. In the FDR row, ACV and CV stay near 0.5, while BIC and EBIC fall toward 0. In the time row, the pink ACV line sits well below the other methods, and green CV is highest by orders of magnitude. The eye goes first to the separated time curves in the bottom row.
caption: Evaluation of ACV K-fold, CV K-fold and (extended) BIC in learning large scale KNN graph on sub-Gaussian data on pre-screening.
abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.
